messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Security Guard
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Meera was sixty-six years old when her daughter Priya was hit by a car on a Tuesday afternoon in October. The driver had run a red light on the corner of Fifth and Morrison, the same intersection Meera drove through every morning on her way to the security office downtown. Priya, who was thirty-eight, had been crossing to meet her mother for lunch. The impact had thrown her body across the hood of a sedan. By the time Meera arrived at the hospital, Priya had been dead for forty minutes.

In the weeks that followed, Meera had tried to return to work. She was a security guard at a mid-rise office building, a job she had held for twelve years. Her role was to monitor the lobby, check badges, watch the screens. But something had fractured in her that day at the hospital, and it was spreading. Her body had become a thing she no longer trusted. Even sitting at the security desk, her shoulders remained bunched near her ears, her jaw clenched so tightly that her teeth ached by the end of each shift. Her eyes moved constantly—from the elevator to the lobby doors to the windows to the screens—searching for the moment when something would go wrong again, when she would fail to see the danger coming. She had come to believe that if she watched carefully enough, scanned the environment thoroughly enough, perhaps she could prevent the next catastrophe. But the scanning never quieted her; it only exhausted her.

When colleagues would mention a car accident they had heard about on the news, or when someone would describe a fender-bender in the break room, Meera would feel her chest tighten and her hands begin to shake. The words seemed to trigger something physical—a surge of adrenaline that left her trembling. She would excuse herself, go to the bathroom, and sit in a stall trying to breathe until the sensation passed. After a few months of this, she began to avoid the break room altogether, eating her lunch alone in her car in the parking garage. Then she stopped eating lunch at all.

The hardest part was that the memory of that day did not feel like something that had happened in the past. When it returned—and it returned constantly, unbidden, without warning—it felt as though the accident were occurring in the present moment. She could feel the phone call from the hospital, could feel the drive there, could feel the weight of her daughter's absence in the room. The memory was more vivid, more real than any ordinary memory she possessed. It was as if her mind had burned that single day into her consciousness in a way that made everything else seem pale and distant by comparison.

Meera had begun to suppress the thoughts whenever they arose. She would push them away, would distract herself with work tasks or television or anything that required her attention. But the suppression came at a cost. She had withdrawn from her husband, Rajesh, who had also lost his daughter. When he tried to talk about his grief, or when he suggested they attend a memorial service for a family friend, Meera would feel a panic rising in her chest. Anything that reminded her of loss—a cemetery she had to drive past, a funeral announcement in the community bulletin—sent her into a state of dread so complete that she would rearrange her entire schedule to avoid it. She had missed her sister's birthday dinner because the restaurant was near a cemetery. She had made excuses to Rajesh about why she could not attend his colleague's funeral.

What tormented her most was the conviction that she had caused this. If she had not suggested lunch that day, if she had chosen a different restaurant, if she had left the office five minutes earlier or later, the timing would have been different. She should have known something was wrong. She should have protected her daughter. The fact that she had not—the fact that she had failed in the most fundamental way a mother could fail—had convinced her that she would never again feel the normal, uncomplicated emotions she had once known. Grief had taken permanent residence in her, and she was certain now that joy and peace were simply no longer available to her.

It was Rajesh who finally insisted she see someone. He had found her sitting in the dark one evening, unable to move, unable to explain why. He made the appointment himself.
